moves.spoken: We have White and open the pawn to e4, met by e5.
The knight to f3.
Black develops the knight to c6. We could play many things here — the Scotch, the Italian.
Let's play the Scotch — in fact the Scotch Gambit, with the pawn to d4.
Black captures on d4. The Scotch Gambit is a cross between a Scotch and an Italian.
The bishop to c4 — an opening that slips through the cracks. A great alternative if you play the Evans Gambit: super dangerous at this level, played by grandmasters, a completely legitimate weapon.
Black plays the pawn to d6. There are a bunch of traps here that bring quick wins, and d6 leads to a slightly worse but solid position — a good way to sidestep the traps.
Think of it like the Italian — you play this first largely to open your access to the g5-square.
Because in many lines the knight or bishop to g5 is a very important aspect.
That g5-square is what the move order is for.
After the capture on d4.

Black recaptures with the knight on d4, giving back the pawn to open the diagonal for the bishop. We have a very nice position — better central control, a bishop on c4 like a good Scotch, and the sacrificed pawn recovered.
Black develops the knight to f6. Now, should we fear a capture on d4 that puts our queen in the centre?
The knight to c3 — and no, no fear: Black has no second knight to bring to c6, so the queen would sit perfectly well placed on d4.
Black plays the bishop to e7 — a Philidor-like, very solid setup, the d6-pawn restraining our e4. Don't lunge at Black's throat here.
We castle — nurture the advantage, bring the pieces out, and enjoy the space and well-placed pieces.

Black castles — and it's trickier than it looks. The pawn to f4 is premature with the queen undeveloped. The bishop to e3 or g5 look natural, but both allow tactics: the bishop to e3 runs into the knight to g4, and the center-fork trick — the knight takes e4, then the pawn to d5 recovers the piece with mass trades we don't want.
So the bishop to b3 — it permanently takes the center-fork trick away, tucking the bishop onto a defended square, out of the pawn's reach.
The pawn to f3 is possible but a little weakening — though it's viable, since the bishop to e3 would then cover the weakened diagonal.
We play the bishop to b3 without f3. Black's knight to e5 is odd — it walks into something.
No need for h3 — the pawn to f4: the e5-knight isn't stable, so we kick it and grab more of the centre.
The pawn to f4 was dismissed earlier because it came without tempo — but now that the bishop is on a safer square, it's more justified.
Now we have more central control; we still want to complete development, though the immediate bishop to e3 might run into the knight to g4.

Black plays the bishop to g4 — don't be intimidated: it attacks the queen but that's all, and the bishop can get into real trouble. Where to put the queen? d2 is awkward, d3 is covered by the knight — so the queen to e1, which can later swing to g3 to x-ray the king and doesn't block the bishop. Simple logic, and simple isn't the same as easy.
The queen to e1.
Black plays the knight to d7, anticipating our plans.
The queen to d2 would have blocked the bishop.
The queen to e1 is good because it can later reach g3 to x-ray the king.

The pawn to h3 — and the g4-bishop is in trouble. If Black tries the bishop to h5, we push g4, it drops to g6, and f5 corners it. The bishop-to-b6 counter wins the exchange, since after the capture on e6 and the recapture, the knight takes e6 forking king, queen and rook.

Black gives up the bishop, taking on h3. Pushing a pawn in front of our king is justified: Black has no kingside firepower, winning a piece is significant, and the queen can always come to g3 to shelter.
We recapture on h3 — and the queen can also defend from g3, lending the king some cover, like an umbrella.
Black gives up the bishop immediately; the way to extricate it was a counterattack.
The counterattack was the pawn to c5, hitting the knight.
If the knight moves, the bishop can take it — or drop back to e6, now that the square is uncovered — a bit of panic.
Now there's an extra square available for the knight that wasn't there before.

Don't submissively drop the knight back to f3 — think how the position changed: winning the bishop cleared f5 for the knight, and now everything aims at the kingside. A powerful attacking mechanism on top of the extra piece.

We're up a piece and clearly better. The pawn to e5 is great, maybe even best; the queen to g3 threatens mate, which Black must meet with the pawn to g6, not the flimsy knight to h5 — a biting-on-granite situation.
After the pawn to g6, taking there is met by the recapture, since the spot is pinned — but the pawn to e5 is the better way, opening a second front.
We take on e5 — holding the queen to g3 in our pocket while also attacking down the middle; combining the two fronts crushes Black.
We recapture on e5.
Black plays the knight to h5. We can't play the queen to g3, but no matter.
The pawn to e6 — actualizing the b3-bishop. Crushing: we attack the knight and the pawn, and the bishop will fall too, a piece defended only once.

A note on undefended pieces: a type-two undefended piece is protected by only one other piece — never a pawn — while type-one is simply hanging. Black's knight on h5 is hanging, but the d7-knight and the e7-bishop are each defended only once, and opening the e-file exploits that, since the queen is a poor defender. The finish: the obvious pawn to f7, but take the bishop first — if Black recaptures, the pawn takes f7 and wins the queen, or a rook recapture leaves it pinned. Then the pawn takes f7, up two pieces. Consolidate and keep control. Later Black's queen to b6 sets up an x-ray on the king with the threat of the check on c4 — prevent it not passively but by targeting the queen: the queen to e6, using the trade as a weapon, since up two pieces a trade is entirely in our favour. If Black keeps the x-ray with the queen to a7, our queen on e6 is beautifully placed and the bishop to e3 follows. Then complete development, the bishop to g5 — even up two pieces, adhere to principles. As Purdy said, you play to win points, not to paint pictures; don't chase beauty at the cost of a simple win.
Black gives up the rook and resigns.
A quick overview of the Scotch Gambit: after the capture and the bishop to c4, Black has two main moves.
The first is to defend the pawn.
The second is to counterattack White's pawn.
If Black plays the knight to f6.
White plays the pawn to e5, attacking the knight — and Black has a crucial counter.
The pawn to d5, hitting the bishop — the key idea; without it the gambit would refute the knight to f6.
The point is to occupy the centre and open the light-squared bishop; then the bishop to b5 gives a sharp, interesting structure — worth considering even at 2000, and played at grandmaster level.

The second option is the bishop to c5, met by the venomous pawn to c3: after Black captures, the c5-bishop is undefended. Don't play the queen to d5 — the tempting fork fails to the queen to e7 defending both. The bishop to g5 is met by the pawn to f6, and the capture on b2 is a big threat too. So change the move order — take on f7 first with a check and win the pawn: equal material, but Black's king is permanently weak and White has a fun position, though not winning.
That's not a good line for Black — so the knight to f6 is the main move.
Then the pawn to e5 and the pawn to d5.
You reach a position similar to the knight-to-f6 line — rich, tactical, and interesting.

The pawn to d6 is fine and solid. The bishop to b3 stops the center-fork trick. Black's knight to e5 was the root of the problems. The way to handle it as Black: take on d4 and develop the bishop to e6, and when cramped, trade a couple of pieces to ease the burden — that light-squared bishop is a beast. White is better, but Black is solid with no weaknesses; after the pawn to f4, the bishop to g4 is almost the decisive mistake — the pawn to c6 is safer, and the d6-pawn acts as a barrier to e5. And after the bishop to g4, the idea is the pawn to c5 hitting the d4-knight, then the capture on f3 — not losing the bishop — or better, the bishop back to e6: a nasty position for Black, but not down material.
At this level you do need to learn the theory of these basic responses.
Just a couple of moves' worth.
After the capture and the bishop to c4.

If you just know to play the pawn to d5, you get a decent position — improvising from a position of strength works; the trouble comes when you don't know what to do from the start. These days d4 and e4 are considered largely equivalent.
